ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Data collection procedures were approved by the Boston College IRB protocol 16.242.

Child participants were 41.24% White, 22.68% Asian, 15.46% Multiracial, 6.19% Hispanic or Latino, 2.06% Black, 1.03% Native Hawaiian or Pacific Islander, and 11.34% did not report their race or ethnicity.
No socioeconomic data were collected. 98 participants were tested, and n = 1 participant was excluded for desire to discontinue the study (preregistered criterion).
Participants were recruited from a laboratory database and were individually tested over Zoom.
While a few participants were ages 12 (n = 18, 10%) and 15 (n = 2, 1.11%), most participants were ages 13 or 14 (n = 160, 88.89%).
Participants were 59.44% White, 8.33% Multiracial, 5% Native American, 2.22% Black, 2.22% Asian, 0.55% Hispanic or Latino, 0.55% Middle Eastern, and 21.67% did not report race or ethnicity.

Participants were from small, rural, and predominantly White schools whose demographics are similar to roughly 33% of all middle schools in the United States. 277 participants were collected by CLRN to mitigate data quality issues.

Participants were excluded for not completing the survey (n = 45, pre-registered criterion) and for incorrectly answering an attention check question at the end of the protocol (n = 52, preregistered criterion), leaving a final sample of 180.

The preregistered adult sample was collected over Prolific and comprised N = 201 adults ages 18 years or older (Mage = 38.98, SDage= 13.58, min = 18, max = 81) in the United States who were 54.23% female, 43.28% male, 2.49% did not report gender, and were 77.61% White, 10.95% Black, 4.48% Multiracial, 2.99% Hispanic or Latino, 1.49% Asian, and 2.49% did not report race or ethnicity.
We pre-registered with 200 participants, and 205 participants were collected to compensate for Prolific glitches.
Participants were excluded for incorrectly answering an attention check question at the end of the protocol (n = 4, pre-registered criterion).
All other participants completed the survey and answered no more than 1 memory check question incorrectly, leaving a final sample of 201.
The ambiguity was also explicitly emphasized at the end of each vignette and again before participants completed dependent measures.
For child participants, written parental consent and child verbal assent were obtained, while adult participants provided electronic written consent.
Child participants had three opportunities to answer correctly, while adolescents and adults had one.
Participants provided responses for five dependent measures: forgiveness expectation, trust expectation, punishment decision, perpetrator intent, and transgression severity (Table 1).

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Four pre-registrations were written for this project, one for adults (AsPredicted #133834, https://aspredicted.org/hm22-ynjf.pdf), one for adolescents (AsPredicted #146214, https://aspredicted.org/r822-9m5z.pdf), and two for children (AsPredicted #138020, https://aspredicted.org/6cjw-xkrp.pdf; AsPredicted #142454, https://aspredicted.org/p778-ssxp.pdf). The second child preregistration was written to correct some typographical errors in the original preregistration and to add more specific information about how we planned to recruit children based on age. Separate preregistrations were written because data recruitment and collection methods varied for each age group. After data collection, a sensitivity analysis with 5,000 simulations confirmed that our sample was 96.84% (95% CI: 96.32, 97.31) powered to detect three-way interaction effects between perpetrator type, victim type, and age group at = .05.

No socioeconomic data were collected. 98 participants were tested, and n = 1 participant was excluded for desire to discontinue the study (preregistered criterion). Only two participants each failed one out of 16 memory checks, and all observations were included in the final sample.

We pre-registered with 200 participants, and 205 participants were collected to compensate for Prolific glitches. Participants were excluded for incorrectly answering an attention check question at the end of the protocol (n = 4, pre-registered criterion). All other participants completed the survey and answered no more than 1 memory check question incorrectly, leaving a final sample of 201. The adolescent and adult samples were larger than the child sample to provide 80% power to detect a small to medium three-way interaction effect between perpetrator type, victim type, and intent at = .05. These results are reported in the supplemental materials.

table.title: Comparing Interpersonal and Intergroup Forgiveness in an Ambiguous Transgression
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions: Do children think about interpersonal and intergroup forgiveness differently in the context of an ambiguously intentional transgression? Do attributions of intentionality explain differences in expectations about the likelihood of forgiveness between interpersonal and intergroup contexts?
table.design_dependent_variables:
1) Likelihood of Forgiveness: How likely do you think it is that [Victim]* will forgive [Perpetrator]* for [Transgression]*? (1-'Really not likely to 6-Really likely')

 2) Deservingness of Forgiveness: Do you think [Perpetrator] deserves to be forgiven for knocking over and ruining the Lego spaceships? (1-'Really not deserving' to 6-'Really deserving')

 3) Intentionality: Remember, we don't know for sure whether [Transgression] by accident or on purpose. But I want to know what you think. Do you think it happened by accident or on purpose? (1-'Definitely by accident' to 6-'Definitely on purpose')

 4) Victim's Perception of Intentionality: [Victim] saw the Lego spaceships being knocked over and being ruined. I want to know what you think [Victim] believes. Do you think that [Victim] believes that [transgression] by accident or on purpose? (1-'Definitely by accident' to 6-'Definitely on purpose')

 5) Severity: How good or bad was [Transgression]? (1-'Really bad' to 6-'Really good')

 6) Punishment: How much trouble should [Perpetrator] get in for [Transgression]? (1-'No trouble' to 4-'A lot of trouble')
 7) Trust: How good or bad was [Transgression]? (1-'Really not likely' to 6-'Really likely')

 *Transgression, victim, and perpetrator will vary by vignette. All DVs, with the exception of #6, are on a 6-point likert scale.
table.study_design_overview: There are two independent variables (Perpetrator Type, Victim Type) with two levels each (Group, Individual), resulting in four experimental conditions. The four conditions are: Condition 1 (Intergroup): Group perpetrator and group victim; Condition 2: Group perpetrator and individual victim; Condition 3: Individual perpetrator and group victim; Condition 4 (Interpersonal): Individual perpetrator and individual victim. All conditions are within-subjects, and participants will see each condition twice. Participants will see all conditions in a randomized order, and conditions are randomized across vignettes.
table.statistical_tests:
Model 1: To determine whether condition influences expectations about the likelihood of forgiveness, we will run a linear mixed effects model (LMEM) with likelihood of forgiveness as the response term (Continuous: 1-6), condition as the predictor (Categorial: Group perpetrator and group victim, Group perpetrator and individual victim, Individual perpetrator and group victim, and Individual perpetrator and individual victim), and subject and vignette identity as random effects.
 Model 2: To determine whether condition influences expectations about the deservingness of forgiveness, we will run a linear mixed effects model (LMEM) with deservingness of forgiveness as the response term (Continuous: 1-6), condition as the predictor (Categorial: Group perpetrator and group victim, Group perpetrator and individual victim, Individual perpetrator and group victim, and Individual perpetrator and individual victim), and subject and vignette identity as random effects.
 Model 3: To determine whether condition influences expectations about the intentionality of the transgression, we will run a linear mixed effects model (LMEM) with intent as the response term (Continuous: 1-6), condition as the predictor (Categorial: Group perpetrator and group victim, Group perpetrator and individual victim, Individual perpetrator and group victim, and Individual perpetrator and individual victim), and subject and vignette identity as random effects.
 Model 4: To determine whether condition influences expectations about the victim's perception of the intentionality of the transgression, we will run a linear mixed effects model (LMEM) with victim's perception of intentionality as the response term (Continuous: 1-6), condition as the predictor (Categorial: Group perpetrator and group victim, Group perpetrator and individual victim, Individual perpetrator and group victim, and Individual perpetrator and individual victim), and subject and vignette identity as random effects.
 Model 5: To determine whether condition influences expectations about the severity of the transgression, we will run a linear mixed effects model (LMEM) with severity as the response term (Continuous: 1-6), condition as the predictor (Categorial: Group perpetrator and group victim, Group perpetrator and individual victim, Individual perpetrator and group victim, and Individual perpetrator and individual victim), and subject and vignette identity as random effects.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
We will exclude participants who answer the attention check question incorrectly ("If you're paying attention to this question, select 'Somewhat disagree'").
 We will exclude participants who answer any of the comprehension questions incorrectly more than once.
 We will exclude participants who do not finish the survey.

7) How many observations will be collected or what will determine sample size? No need to justify decision, but be precise about exactly how the number will be determined.
We will aim to collect a total N of 200 (200 per cell). These numbers are approximate due to our recruitment via Prolific and the possibility that we will need to top up our sample due to exclusions (see Question 6).

8) Anything else you would like to pre-register? (e.g., secondary analyses, variables collected for exploratory purposes, unusual analyses planned?)
We plan on soft launching our survey with N=40 to ensure that our survey and display logic are working correctly - if there are no processing errors in the survey, we will include these data points in our final N.
 Top up procedure: If necessary, to ensure we have the full N of 200, we will top up our sample by re-running the study with the smallest batch possible based on the exclusion rate from the first launch.

 Additional Analyses:
 Model 6: To determine whether condition influences expectations about punishment, we will run a linear mixed effects model (LMEM) with punishment as the response term (Continuous: 1-4), condition as the predictor (Categorial: Group perpetrator and group victim, Group perpetrator and individual victim, Individual perpetrator and group victim, and Individual perpetrator and individual victim), and subject and vignette identity as random effects.
 Model 7: To determine whether condition influences expectations about trust, we will run a linear mixed effects model (LMEM) with trust as the response term (Continuous: 1-6), condition as the predictor (Categorial: Group perpetrator and group victim, Group perpetrator and individual victim, Individual perpetrator and group victim, and Individual perpetrator and individual victim), and subject and vignette identity as random effects.

 Forgiveness Models
 Model 8: To determine whether intent and condition influence expectations about the likelihood of forgiveness, we will run a linear mixed effects model (LMEM) with likelihood of forgiveness as the response term (Continuous: 1-6), intent as a predictor (Continuous: 1-6), condition as a predictor (Categorial: Group perpetrator and group victim, Group perpetrator and individual victim, Individual perpetrator and group victim, and Individual perpetrator and individual victim), and subject and vignette identity as random effects.
 Model 9: To determine whether severity, intent, and condition influence expectations about the likelihood of forgiveness, we will run a linear mixed effects model (LMEM) with likelihood of forgiveness as the response term (Continuous: 1-6), severity as a predictor (Continuous: 1-6), intent as a predictor (Continuous: 1-6), condition as a predictor (Categorial: Group perpetrator and group victim, Group perpetrator and individual victim, Individual perpetrator and group victim, and Individual perpetrator and individual victim), and subject and vignette identity as random effects.
 Model 10: To determine whether model 1, model 8, or model 9 accounts for more variance in likelihood of forgiveness, we will run r-squared difference tests between model 1 and model 8 and then between model 8 and model 9.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

info.title: Differing Conceptions of Interpersonal and Intergroup Conflict Resolution Across the Lifespan

text.text: Children ages 5-10 years, adolescents ages 12-15 years, and adults viewed interpersonal (individual vs. individual) and intergroup (group vs. group) conflicts with ambiguous perpetrator intent.
Participants perceived more intentionality and expected harsher responses in intergroup conflicts than in interpersonal conflicts; this effect strengthened within childhood and between age groups.
Greater intentionality was attributed to group perpetrators than individual perpetrators which accounted for harsher response expectations in intergroup relative to interpersonal conflicts.
Different conceptions of interpersonal and intergroup conflict resolution emerge early in development and increasingly diverge across the lifespan.
Conflicts pervade social interactions across development.

From the playground to the office to the battlefield, conflicts foment distrust, cause emotional, financial, and physical harms, and threaten the social bonds necessary for thriving relationships and cooperative societies (Bar-Tal, 2011; Lewicki et al., 2021).
text.formatted: From the playground to the office to the battlefield, conflicts foment distrust, cause emotional, financial, and physical harms, and threaten the social bonds necessary for thriving relationships and cooperative societies <ref type="bibr">(Bar-Tal, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Lewicki et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Conflict resolution is therefore required to ameliorate these harms and sustain cooperative relationships (Laursen et al., 2001; Taylor, 2020).
text.formatted: Conflict resolution is therefore required to ameliorate these harms and sustain cooperative relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Laursen et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Taylor, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: However, successfully resolving conflict is challenging because it involves complex social processes like forgiving, restoring justice, and rebuilding trust (McAuliffe et al., 2025; McLaughlin et al., 2024; Reinders Folmer et al., 2021).
text.formatted: However, successfully resolving conflict is challenging because it involves complex social processes like forgiving, restoring justice, and rebuilding trust <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(McAuliffe et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">McLaughlin et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Reinders Folmer et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Conflict resolution is also difficult because conflicts are multifaceted and complex.

They can vary in topic (e.g., resources, ideology, status), participants (e.g., siblings, friend groups, political parties), and scale (e.g., interpersonal, local, domestic, international), among other dimensions (Bar-Tal, 2011; Lewicki et al., 2021).
text.formatted: They can vary in topic (e.g., resources, ideology, status), participants (e.g., siblings, friend groups, political parties), and scale (e.g., interpersonal, local, domestic, international), among other dimensions <ref type="bibr">(Bar-Tal, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Lewicki et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, effective conflict resolution requires first identifying the most impactful elements of conflicts and investigating how those elements affect conceptions of and responses to conflict.
One approach to characterizing different types of conflict has been to distinguish between interpersonal and intergroup conflicts.
In this framework, interpersonal conflicts concern character traits or personal preferences, while intergroup conflicts concern group membership (Killen et al., 2013; Stephan, 2008; Verkuyten, 2022).
text.formatted: In this framework, interpersonal conflicts concern character traits or personal preferences, while intergroup conflicts concern group membership <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Killen et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Stephan, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Verkuyten, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: For example, a conflict would be interpersonal if one coworker insulted another coworker because of their rude behavior, but it would be intergroup if it was because of their religion.
While apology, forgiveness, or punishment can help resolve interpersonal conflicts, intergroup conflict resolution must also address group membership (Böhm et al., 2020).
text.formatted: While apology, forgiveness, or punishment can help resolve interpersonal conflicts, intergroup conflict resolution must also address group membership <ref type="bibr">(Böhm et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This framework identified conflict content as critical for understanding conflicts and has generated more targeted prejudice reduction interventions (e.g., Confer et al., 2025; Killen et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This framework identified conflict content as critical for understanding conflicts and has generated more targeted prejudice reduction interventions <ref type="bibr">(e.g., Confer et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Killen et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond conflict content, however, interpersonal and intergroup conflicts also differ in that they have different types of perpetrators and victims (Enright et al., 2016; Wildschut & Insko, 2007).
text.formatted: Beyond conflict content, however, interpersonal and intergroup conflicts also differ in that they have different types of perpetrators and victims <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Enright et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Wildschut & Insko, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: In this framework, interpersonal conflicts are between an individual perpetrator and an individual victim, whereas intergroup conflicts are between a group perpetrator and a group victim.
For example, if one coworker insulted another coworker, even about their religion, the conflict would be interpersonal because it has an individual perpetrator and an individual victim.
But, if a group of coworkers insulted another group of coworkers, even about their rude behavior, the conflict would be intergroup because it has a group perpetrator and a group victim.

Independent of conflict content, defining conflicts by their actors provides an orthogonal lens through which to understand and evaluate the differences between these conflicts (Wildschut & Insko, 2025; Van Lange & Bergmann, 2026).
text.formatted: Independent of conflict content, defining conflicts by their actors provides an orthogonal lens through which to understand and evaluate the differences between these conflicts <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Wildschut & Insko, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Van Lange & Bergmann, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The type of perpetrator and victim (i.e., individual or group) likely impacts conceptions of conflict and its resolution.
Individuals and groups are different; they have different cognitive, affective, and social capacities (Enright et al., 2016; Van Lange & Bergmann, 2026).
text.formatted: Individuals and groups are different; they have different cognitive, affective, and social capacities <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Enright et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Van Lange & Bergmann, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: An individual has one mind and consults only their own thoughts and feelings when evaluating, initiating, or responding to conflicts.

In contrast, a group comprises many individuals, each with their own mind and emotions, making conflict more complex for groups to navigate and harder for observers to attribute mental states (Van Lange & Bergmann, 2026).
text.formatted: In contrast, a group comprises many individuals, each with their own mind and emotions, making conflict more complex for groups to navigate and harder for observers to attribute mental states <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Van Lange & Bergmann, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These differences matter because they may impact perceptions of intent and severity which are important in shaping conceptions of conflict (Ames & Fiske, 2013; Amir et al., 2021; Wildschut & Insko, 2007).
text.formatted: These differences matter because they may impact perceptions of intent and severity which are important in shaping conceptions of conflict <ref type="bibr">(Ames & Fiske, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Amir et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Wildschut & Insko, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: For example, individual perpetrators could be perceived as more intentional because they act independently so their intent is concentrated, whereas groups require coordination, so their intent is diffused among group members (Cooley et al., 2017).
text.formatted: For example, individual perpetrators could be perceived as more intentional because they act independently so their intent is concentrated, whereas groups require coordination, so their intent is diffused among group members <ref type="bibr">(Cooley et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Alternatively, group perpetrators may be perceived as more intentional because unified collective action requires intentional coordination between all group members, whereas an individual does not coordinate with others, so their actions may be more likely to be deemed accidental relative to a group (Waytz & Young, 2012).
text.formatted: Alternatively, group perpetrators may be perceived as more intentional because unified collective action requires intentional coordination between all group members, whereas an individual does not coordinate with others, so their actions may be more likely to be deemed accidental relative to a group <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Waytz & Young, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Further, relative to an individual victim, harming a group may be perceived as especially severe because more people are harmed (Riggs & Kalish, 2016; Singer, 2015).
text.formatted: Further, relative to an individual victim, harming a group may be perceived as especially severe because more people are harmed <ref type="bibr">(Riggs & Kalish, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Singer, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, relative to a group, harming an individual might be considered more severe because they are more vulnerable than a group (Nordgren & McDonnell, 2011).
text.formatted: In contrast, relative to a group, harming an individual might be considered more severe because they are more vulnerable than a group <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Nordgren & McDonnell, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, whether a perpetrator or victim is an individual or group likely impacts perceptions of and responses to interpersonal and intergroup conflicts, with downstream effects for conflict resolution.
A developmental approach is particularly well-positioned to examine how conceptions of interpersonal and intergroup conflicts may differ.
From a young age, children begin developing the capacity for conflict resolution (Laursen et al., 2001; Nasie et al., 2016).
text.formatted: From a young age, children begin developing the capacity for conflict resolution <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Laursen et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Nasie et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Like adults, children respond to conflicts by forgiving, punishing, and establishing trust, and they anticipate more positive outcomes after forgiveness and more negative outcomes after punishment or inaction (Amir et al., 2021; Kinzler et al., 2011; McAuliffe et al., 2025; Loustau et al., 2024; McLaughlin et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Like adults, children respond to conflicts by forgiving, punishing, and establishing trust, and they anticipate more positive outcomes after forgiveness and more negative outcomes after punishment or inaction <ref type="bibr">(Amir et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Kinzler et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">McAuliffe et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Loustau et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">McLaughlin et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Children as young as 5 years old reject stereotypes as the basis for social exclusion and rectify group-based inequalities (Elenbaas et al., 2016; Killen & Stangor, 2001).
text.formatted: Children as young as 5 years old reject stereotypes as the basis for social exclusion and rectify group-based inequalities <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Elenbaas et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Killen & Stangor, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Children also expect more trust after forgiveness than adolescents or adults (McLaughlin et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Children also expect more trust after forgiveness than adolescents or adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(McLaughlin et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These findings underscore that conceptions of conflict are present in childhood and develop with age.
relevant for differentiating between interpersonal and intergroup contexts.

Specifically, theory of mind and intent attribution emerge in childhood and strengthen into adolescence and adulthood (Buon & Margoni, 2025; Dumontheil et al., 2010; Guazzelli Williamson et al., 2025; Killen et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Specifically, theory of mind and intent attribution emerge in childhood and strengthen into adolescence and adulthood <ref type="bibr">(Buon & Margoni, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Dumontheil et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Guazzelli Williamson et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Killen et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: If, as argued, perspective taking and intent perceptions operate differently for individual and group perpetrators, we would expect to see distinct developmental patterns for interpersonal and intergroup conflicts.

Exploring interpersonal and intergroup conflicts as these cognitive abilities emerge can test our hypotheses and provide insight into the developmental processes underpinning responses to these conflicts.
Children also develop complex group cognition throughout childhood (Liberman et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Children also develop complex group cognition throughout childhood <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Liberman et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Infants stare longer at ingroup than outgroup members, exhibiting the precursors of intergroup cognition (Fogiel et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Infants stare longer at ingroup than outgroup members, exhibiting the precursors of intergroup cognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Fogiel et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: With age, children increasingly understand whether individuals belong to a group, perceive different levels of entitativity between different groups, and distinguish between groups and collections of individuals (Plötner et al., 2016; Svirydzenka et al., 2010).
text.formatted: With age, children increasingly understand whether individuals belong to a group, perceive different levels of entitativity between different groups, and distinguish between groups and collections of individuals <ref type="bibr">(Plötner et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Svirydzenka et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: They also make different inferences about larger and smaller groups, perceive status differences, and use group membership information to make inferences about social preferences (Heck et al., 2022).
text.formatted: They also make different inferences about larger and smaller groups, perceive status differences, and use group membership information to make inferences about social preferences <ref type="bibr">(Heck et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Because the antecedents of complex group cognition emerge in childhood, children can likely differentiate between individual and group perpetrators and victims, which may in turn lead to distinct developmental trajectories for conceptions of interpersonal and intergroup conflicts.
However, this has not yet been demonstrated empirically, and how conceptions of and responses to interpersonal and intergroup conflicts develop remains an open question.
We investigated the development of conceptions of and responses to interpersonal and intergroup conflicts in children, adolescents, and adults.
Participants viewed third-person interpersonal (individual perpetrator and victim) and intergroup (group perpetrator and victim) transgression vignettes.
They also viewed vignettes with a group perpetrator and an individual victim as well as with an individual perpetrator and a group victim.

This design allowed us to examine differences between interpersonal and intergroup conflict, isolate the independent effects of perpetrator type and victim type, and detect interactions between our manipulations.
In attribute intent differently to individuals and groups.

Participants then reported perceptions of and responses to conflict including perceptions of perpetrator intent, perceptions of transgression severity, expectations of forgiveness, expectations of trust, and punishment decisions.
Following prior work (e.g., McLaughlin et al., 2024), forgiveness and punishment were used because they are familiar responses to conflict for children and adults.
text.formatted: Following prior work (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">McLaughlin et al., 2024)</ref>, forgiveness and punishment were used because they are familiar responses to conflict for children and adults.

text.text: Trust was measured because it is an important facilitator of conflict resolution (Reinders Folmer et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Trust was measured because it is an important facilitator of conflict resolution <ref type="bibr">(Reinders Folmer et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Perceptions of intent and severity were measured because they are commonly evaluated when considering responses to conflict, and they are central to our hypotheses (Ames & Fiske, 2013; Nordgren & McDonnell, 2011).
text.formatted: Perceptions of intent and severity were measured because they are commonly evaluated when considering responses to conflict, and they are central to our hypotheses <ref type="bibr">(Ames & Fiske, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Nordgren & McDonnell, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: This design enabled us to address four primary research questions: 1.
Are interpersonal and intergroup conflicts perceived and responded to differently?
What is the effect of age within childhood and between age groups?
What are the effects of perpetrator type and victim type?
Are there mediating effects of intent and severity?
We anticipated that answering these questions would provide new insight into how conflict and its resolution are conceptualized across the lifespan.

This study had a 2(Perpetrator type: individual, group) by 2(Victim type: individual, group) by 3(Age group: child, adolescent, adult) factorial design with first two factors withinsubjects and the third factor between-subjects (Figure 1).

text.text: The crossing of the within-subject factors resulted in four experimental conditions: interpersonal (individual perpetrator and individual victim), intergroup (group perpetrator and group victim), and two mixed conditions: group perpetrator and individual victim, and individual perpetrator and group victim (Figure 1).

Participants saw each condition twice in a randomized order, for a total of 8 vignettes per participant (birdhouses, carrots, school projects, flowers, games, kites, Lego bricks, tomato plants).

text.text: To examine the effects of perpetrator type, victim type, and age group on each dependent measure, we ran linear mixedeffects models with the dependent variable as the response term (continuous), perpetrator type (categorical: individual, group), victim type (categorical: individual, group), age group (categorical: child, adolescent, adult), their interactions, gender, and vignette order as predictors with subject and vignette content as random effects.

All contrasts were conducted using this model, and post-hoc tests used the multivariate t (MVT) p-value correction method for multiple comparisons, which does not assume that contrasts are independent.
Degrees of freedom were calculated using the Satterthwaite method.
Severity was reverse-coded for all analyses.
While we preregistered running separate models for each age group, running one model reduced experiment-wise error by minimizing the number of models and post-hoc contrasts.
All hypotheses were tested using this model except for the within-childhood age-related effects.

To analyze within-childhood age differences, we ran linear mixed-effects models for each dependent measure with the dependent variable as the response term (continuous), perpetrator type (categorical: individual, group), victim type (categorical: individual, group), age (continuous), their interactions, gender, and vignette order as predictors with subject and vignette content as random effects.
Age was calculated as the difference between participation dates and participant birthdays.
We did not preregister analyses treating age as continuous across all age groups because we expected most of the developmental change to occur in childhood.
We were unable to collect adolescent and adult birthdays.

To test whether intent and severity mediated the relations between our manipulations and responses to conflict, we ran three multigroup structural equation models: intent as sole mediator, severity as sole mediator, and a parallel mediation model.
The models used full information maximum likelihood estimation with cluster robust standard errors to account for the within-subjects design and cluster randomized vignette order.

Adolescents and adults punished group perpetrators more than individual perpetrators, while adults also perceived greater severity when the perpetrator was a group rather than an individual.

Overall, perpetrator type was a strong predictor of the dependent measures within each age group, suggesting that perpetrator type plays an important role in explaining differences between approaches to interpersonal and intergroup conflicts.
Although no main effects of victim type were observed in any age group, victim type moderated the relationships between perpetrator type and some dependent measures.

No significant interactions emerged for children, but adolescents and adults both expected the least forgiveness and perceived the most intent and severity when a group perpetrator harmed an individual victim.

text.text: Beginning in childhood, conflicts are common across a range of social relationships.
Maintaining these relationships requires effective conflict resolution, which in turn, involves identifying and responding to the most important elements of a particular conflict.

This study proposed that evaluating conflicts by their perpetrators (individual vs. group) and victims (individual vs. group) provided a new lens for investigating how conflicts are conceptualized and responded to.

Participants evaluated and responded to intergroup conflicts (group perpetrator and group victim) more harshly than interpersonal conflicts (individual perpetrator and individual victim), and this pattern increased with age.
Notably, these were differences in degree as opposed to direction, suggesting that intergroup conflicts are considered more extreme than, but not radically distinct, from interpersonal conflicts.
E i i i iconflicts were largely driven by the perception that group perpetrators are more intentional than individual perpetrators.
Intent perceptions explained, across all age groups (forgiveness and trust approached significance for children), why participants responded more harshly in intergroup conflicts.
Notably, intent was a stronger and more consistent mediator than severity for all age groups, indicating that intent, rather than severity, was more impactful when evaluating conflicts.

Alternatively, fewer severity effects may have been detected because the severity measure had relatively low variability on its six-pointscale (SD = .77; SDchild = .94; SDadolescent = .77; SDadult = .68).

However, there were still significant effects for severity in adolescents and adults, increasing the likelihood that severity was genuinely less impactful than intent in shaping conceptions of conflict.

While not independently impactful, victim type interacted with perpetrator type in adolescence and adulthood such that conflicts with a group perpetrator and an individual victim were viewed as most extreme.

These findings may have occurred because individual victims were perceived as more vulnerable than group victims, with the power imbalance between perpetrator and victim amplifying perceptions of intent and severity (Nordgren & McDonnell, 2011).
text.formatted: These findings may have occurred because individual victims were perceived as more vulnerable than group victims, with the power imbalance between perpetrator and victim amplifying perceptions of intent and severity <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Nordgren & McDonnell, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Given that these effects were not observed in children, the ability to coordinate information about perpetrators and victims and consider the vulnerability of individual victims may emerge later in development.

Separately, when there was a group victim, children, with age, perceived more intent and expected less trust, illustrating that while children increasingly become sensitive to victim type, they interpret its impact in the opposite direction from adolescents and adults.
Instead, children may more simplistically infer that harming a group victim is worse because more people are harmed (Riggs & Kalish, 2016; Singer, 2015).
text.formatted: Instead, children may more simplistically infer that harming a group victim is worse because more people are harmed <ref type="bibr">(Riggs & Kalish, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Singer, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these findings highlight that perpetrator type and, to a lesser extent, victim type, shape perceptions of conflict and expected responses to conflict.
While differences emerged because participants viewed group perpetrators as more intentional than individuals, the reasons for this effect remain unclear.
One possibility is that, as hypothesized, if a group acts collectively, it might be assumed that group members coordinated, leading to higher intent attributions.
Participants may also reason that collective action is unlikely to occur by chance and that if groups act together, it is likely that they acted purposefully.
While not tested directly, these explanations provide potential cognitive mechanisms for the observed developmental change.

Developing Theory of Mind, perspectivetaking, and quantitative reasoning skills may enable children and adolescents to understand the complex dynamics of group cognition and to think probabilistically about collective action, leading them to perceive group actors as more intentional (Crimston et al., 2023; Killen et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Developing Theory of Mind, perspectivetaking, and quantitative reasoning skills may enable children and adolescents to understand the complex dynamics of group cognition and to think probabilistically about collective action, leading them to perceive group actors as more intentional <ref type="bibr">(Crimston et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Killen et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Research examining the relation between cognitive development and conflict resolution could shed light on these findings.
Our study has several limitations.
Our findings apply to well-defined groups of a few people, but they may not hold for larger more amorphous groups like ethnic or political groups.
For a friend group or army unit, the actors are clearly defined, but for ethnic or political groups it is unclear who is acting or being acted upon.
Similar differences may exist between interpersonal conflicts and conflicts involving these types of groups, but this study was not designed to address that question.
Further, real-life conflicts are saturated with social information, but our vignettes were third-person, limited information about intent, and paused before the victims could respond,

This study documents that children have distinct conceptions of and responses to interpersonal and intergroup conflicts, underscoring that conceptions of conflict resolution emerge early in development.
Second, given that intergroup conflicts were approached more harshly than interpersonal conflicts, intergroup conflicts may be perceived as harder to resolve.
Especially considering the ambiguously intentional context, this belief may unnecessarily lead to a skepticism that intergroup conflicts can be resolved, perhaps revealing a bias.
Finally, with age, children perceived more intent and expected less trust.
However, children still perceived less intent and expected more forgiveness and trust than adolescents and adults, independent of condition.
Whether this is because children give more benefit of the doubt, are still developing cognitively, or are more naive, conflict resolution may be easier to facilitate in childhood.
Taken together, this study presents initial evidence that intergroup conflict resolution interventions might be especially impactful in childhood.
From the playground to the battlefield, conflict is a part of life.
Investigating conceptions of conflict, how they are responded to, and, by extension, how they can be resolved is key to understanding this important aspect of the human experience.
This study provides evidence that the type of perpetrators and victims in a conflict impacts conceptions of and responses to conflict.

Because of these differences, interpersonal and intergroup conflicts may require slightly different approaches for their resolution to account for elevated perceptions of intent for group perpetrators.
Given that conceptions of conflict and its resolution begin to emerge in childhood, conflict resolution interventions may be especially effective if implemented as these conceptions are forming.

text.text: During stimuli creation, we needed to develop eight ambiguously intentional transgression vignettes to show all four conditions twice without repeating vignette content.
Participants were N = 184 adults (Mage = 41.3, SDage = 12.6, 57.1% male, 42.4% female) recruited using Prolific.
To minimize perceived differences between the vignettes, we created language for 37 potential scenarios.
The language was displayed without images.

We then normed them across 8 dimensions: intentionality, severity, morality, responsibility, weirdness, punishment, forgiveness, and commonness, each on a sliding scale from 0-100 with higher scores indicating greater magnitude on that dimension.
Each participant rated 10 vignettes on these dimensions in a randomized order.
For each dimension, we ran a one-way ANOVA with the dimension as the outcome and the vignettes as the predictor.
We then ran all post-hoc contrasts with tukey corrections and selected groups of vignettes which did not differ significantly.
Given our interest in creating ambiguously intentional vignettes, we first normed on intentionality and selected vignettes closest to the neutral mid-point of the scale.
Overall, participants thought the transgressions were not very intentional (M = 35.4, SD = 30.3).
The ANOVA was significant F(36, 1803) = 8.04, p < .001.
text.formatted: The ANOVA was significant F(36, 1803) = 8.04, p < .001.

text.text: The group of vignettes which were closest to the neutral mid-point and did not significantly differ were: painting, art, diorama, carrots, kites, tomato plant, birdhouse, flower, science, lego, sculpture, games, snowmen.
The intentionality ratings for this group ranged from 38.4 (painting) to 59.5 (snowmen).
We then took these vignettes and normed them on severity to minimize perceived differences in the severity of the transgressions.
Overall, participants thought these transgressions were not very severe (M = 40.2, SD = 27.9).
The ANOVA was significant F(12, 651) = 14.09, p < .001.
text.formatted: The ANOVA was significant F(12, 651) = 14.09, p < .001.

text.text: The group of vignettes which did not significantly differ were: games, kites, flower, tomato plant, lego, birdhouse, carrots, diorama.
The severity ratings for this group ranged from 28.8 (games) to 39.9 (diorama).
After norming for intentionality and severity, only eight vignettes remained, and these were used for the study.
The diorama vignette was changed to use "school project" instead of "diorama" to be more accessible to children.

These eight vignettes did not differ on morality (F(7, 400) = 0.83, p = .567), responsibility (F(7, 400) = 0.46, p = .862), punishment (F(7, 400) = 1.03, p = .408), or forgiveness, (F(7, 400) = 0.37, p = .919).

There was a significant difference in weirdness (F(7, 400) = 2.44, p = .019) such that ruining a birdhouse was deemed more weird than ruining boardgames, but neither scenario was considered particularly weird.

There were also significant differences in commonness (F(7, 400) = 10.97, p < .001), but these differences were not particularly relevant to our design and were controlled for with condition randomization across vignette.

text.text: We investigated the three-way interaction between perpetrator type, victim type, and intent for forgiveness, trust, and punishment.
These analyses were run separately for children, adolescents, and adults.
We powered for these analyses with the adolescent and adult samples but not for children.
For forgiveness, there were no three-way interactions for children or adolescents.
In adults, independent of condition, intent predicted forgiveness, b = -0.47, t(1533.83) = -23.62, p < .001.

In addition to the variables described in the main text, the adolescent and adult surveys contained two more dependent measures: forgiveness deservingness and character intent.
These measures shifted the evaluative perspective between participants' own judgments and their inferences about the vignette characters' perspectives.

Specifically, while the forgiveness variable measured participant expectations that the victim would forgive the perpetrator, forgiveness deservingness measured participants' own judgements about whether the perpetrator deserved to be forgiven.
Similarly, while the intent variable measured participants' own perceptions of intent, character intent measured participants' beliefs about the victims' intent perceptions.
These measures were presented in a randomized order alongside the other dependent measures.
These measures were not included in the child survey to minimize the protocol length and because they patterned similarly to the forgiveness and intent measures.

text.text: We ran the same analyses on these variables as the analyses in the main text.
We first compared our full model to a null model to test whether our hypothesized predictors improved model fit.
Our hypothesized predictors improved model fit for forgiveness deservingness (χ²(7) = 168.75, p < .001) and character intent (χ²(7) = 90.70, p < .001).
text.formatted: Our hypothesized predictors improved model fit for forgiveness deservingness (χ²(7) = 168.75, p < .001) and character intent (χ²(7) = 90.70, p < .001).

text.text: There was no difference in adolescent and adult forgiveness deservingness (b = 0.00, t(373.85) = 0.01, p = .990) or character intent (b = -0.11, t(372.15) = -1.61, p = .108).
These effects had the same directionality as forgiveness and intent.

Using Welch's independent samples t-tests, we compared differences between forgiveness and forgiveness deservingness and between intent and character intent.

Participants believed perpetrators deserved more forgiveness than the perpetrators were likely to receive (t(5801.70) = 12.27, p < .001), while participants also perceived less intent than they believed the victims perceived (t(5777.10) = -16.77, p < .001).

text.text: These findings suggest that thirdperson judgements and perceptions are less extreme than individuals' perceptions of actors' perspectives in a transgression.
